title: Finite Galois normalization with trivial inertia is finite etale
statement: Let $X$ be an integral scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] whose local rings are integrally closed domains [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], with function field $K=\mathcal O_{X,\eta}$. Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension, meaning finite-dimensional, separable and normal [def-pc-field-extension], and put $\Gamma=\operatorname{Aut}_K(L)$. For every nonempty affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X$, let $B_V$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Suppose that for every such $V$ and every prime $\mathfrak q\subset B_V$ the subgroup $\{h\in\Gamma:h\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q,\ h|_{\operatorname{Frac}(B_V/\mathfrak q)}=1\}$ is trivial. Then $B_V^\Gamma=A$ and $\operatorname{Spec}B_V\to V$ is finite etale [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-weil-etale-morphism] for every $V$. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}L\to X$ through the generic point is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and its relative normalization $Y\to X$ [lem-weil-pbc-relative-normalization], whose inverse image over $V$ is $\operatorname{Spec}B_V$, is finite etale with generic fibre canonically $\operatorname{Spec}L$. For any separable closure $\Omega/K$ [def-pd-separable-closure] containing $L$, and algebraic closure $\widetilde\Omega$ of $\Omega$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], evaluation identifies the geometric generic fibre $|Y_{\operatorname{Spec}\widetilde\Omega}|$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_K(L,\Omega)$, equivariantly for $G=\operatorname{Aut}_K(\Omega)$, where $\sigma\in G$ acts on a lift $t:\operatorname{Spec}\widetilde\Omega\to Y$ by $t\mapsto t\circ\operatorname{Spec}(\widetilde\sigma)$, with $\widetilde\sigma$ the unique extension of $\sigma$ to $\widetilde\Omega$, and on $\operatorname{Hom}_K(L,\Omega)$ by $\phi\mapsto\sigma\circ\phi$. The stabilizer of the point given by the inclusion $L\subset\Omega$ is $\operatorname{Aut}_L(\Omega)$. No Noetherian, excellence, or prior finiteness-of-normalization hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0BTD, lemma-normal-pione-quotient-inertia, final normalization argument; Tag 0BST, lemma-inertia-invariants-etale, applied with trivial inertia.

proof.text: Fix a nonempty affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$. The affine function-field lemma makes $A$ a domain and identifies $K=\mathcal O_{X,\eta}$ with $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ through the germ map. For each prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, the canonical affine local-ring identification is $A_{\mathfrak p}\cong\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p}$. These rings are integrally closed domains by hypothesis, so $A$ is a normal ring by its definition. The theorem on normal rings being integrally closed in their total fraction rings, applied to this domain $A$, now says that $A$ is integrally closed in $K$.

source.place: Tag 034M, lemma-normal-ring-integrally-closed; properties.tex, lemma-locally-normal; schemes.tex, affine local-ring identifications.

proof.text: Write $B=B_V$. The finite Galois fixed-field theorem gives finiteness of $\Gamma$ and $L^\Gamma=K$. Each $h\in\Gamma$ carries $B$ to itself: applying $h$ to a monic equation over $A$ leaves its coefficients fixed, and applying $h^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion. Thus it acts by ring automorphisms. If $b\in B^\Gamma$, then $b\in K$ by the fixed-field theorem, and its monic equation over $A$ implies $b\in A$ by step 1. Conversely every element of $A$ is fixed. Therefore $B^\Gamma=A$. The map $A\to B$ is integral by the definition of integral closure.

source.place: Tag 0BTD, lemma-normal-pione-quotient-inertia, normalization paragraph; fields.tex Tags 09I1 and 09DW for the finite Galois fixed-field theorem.

proof.text: For any prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$, apply the finite-group inertia-invariants theorem with $R=B$ and the action of step 2. Its inertia subgroup is exactly the subgroup in the hypothesis, hence $I=\{1\}$ and $B^I=B$, while $B^\Gamma=A$. It follows that $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is etale on an open neighbourhood of $\mathfrak q$. These neighbourhoods cover $\operatorname{Spec}B$, so the morphism is etale. No finiteness of $B$ has been used. Etaleness implies local finite presentation; the affine-open finite-presentation theorem therefore gives that $B$ is finitely presented over $A$. Together with integrality from step 2, the integral-finite-presentation lemma makes $B$ a finite $A$-module. By the definition of a finite morphism, the displayed affine morphism is finite etale.

source.place: Tag 0BST, lemma-inertia-invariants-etale; morphisms.tex Tag 01TQ, lemma-locally-finite-presentation-characterize; algebra.tex Tag 02JJ, lemma-characterize-finite-in-terms-of-integral.

proof.text: Let $f:\operatorname{Spec}L\to X$ be the stated generic-point morphism. Every nonempty affine open of $X$ contains $\eta$ by the affine function-field lemma, so its inverse image under $f$ is the one-point affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}L$; the empty open has empty inverse image. Thus $f$ is quasi-compact. For its diagonal, the inverse image of any affine open in $\operatorname{Spec}L\times_X\operatorname{Spec}L$ is an open subset of the one-point space $\operatorname{Spec}L$, hence either empty or a singleton and quasi-compact. This proves quasi-separatedness directly from the diagonal definition. Apply relative normalization to $f$: it produces $\nu:Y\to X$ integral, and over each nonempty $V$ its affine description is exactly $\operatorname{Spec}B_V\to\operatorname{Spec}A$, including the inclusion of $B_V$ in $L$. These descriptions and step 3 show that $\nu$ is finite etale: the finite condition holds on every affine open by its definition, and local finite presentation, flatness and unramifiedness are the etale conditions checked on the displayed affine charts.

source.place: Tag 0BTD, lemma-normal-pione-quotient-inertia, normalization paragraph; morphisms.tex Tags 035F, 035H and 035I for relative normalization.

proof.text: Over the generic point in $V$, the affine fibre-product theorem gives the fibre ring $B_V\otimes_A K$. For $S=A\setminus\{0\}$ this is $S^{-1}B_V$: the inverse ring maps are $b\otimes(a/s)\mapsto ab/s$ and $b/s\mapsto b\otimes(1/s)$, well defined by the localization relation and tensor relations. Its inclusion in $L$ is injective since $B_V\subset L$ and all $s\in S$ are nonzero. For $\lambda\in L$, take a monic equation $\lambda^n+a_1\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0$ over $K$, and a common denominator $0\ne d\in A$ with $da_i\in A$ for every $i$. Then $d\lambda$ satisfies the monic equation with coefficients $d^i a_i\in A$, so $d\lambda\in B_V$ and $\lambda=(d\lambda)/d\in S^{-1}B_V$. Thus $S^{-1}B_V=L$ and $Y\times_X\operatorname{Spec}K\cong\operatorname{Spec}L$. This isomorphism is induced by the inclusions $B_V\subset L$ and commutes with restriction, so it is canonical and independent of $V$.

source.place: Tag 0BTD, normalization in the finite extension L; algebra.tex Tag 0307, lemma-integral-closure-localize (the denominator-clearing argument written explicitly).

proof.text: The algebraic extension $\widetilde\Omega/\Omega$ is purely inseparable. Indeed, the separable-first theorem expresses it as separable algebraic followed by purely inseparable, and its separable subextension is just $\Omega$: every element generates a finite separable extension, which is trivial because $\Omega$ is separably closed. The algebraic-closure isomorphism theorem, applied to the two $\Omega$-algebra structures on $\widetilde\Omega$ given by the inclusion and by its composite with $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}_K(\Omega)$, extends $\sigma$ to an automorphism $\widetilde\sigma$ of $\widetilde\Omega$. In characteristic $p>0$, two such extensions agree on $a$ because some $a^{p^r}$ belongs to $\Omega$ and the equation $T^{p^r}-\sigma(a^{p^r})=0$ has at most one root in a field. In characteristic zero $\widetilde\Omega=\Omega$. Hence the extension is unique; uniqueness also gives $\widetilde{\sigma\tau}=\widetilde\sigma\widetilde\tau$.

source.place: Tag 030K, lemma-separable-first; algebraic closure existence and uniqueness, applied with a twisted base-field inclusion.

proof.text: By step 5 and the affine fibre-product theorem, the geometric generic fibre is $Z=\operatorname{Spec}(L\otimes_K\widetilde\Omega)$. The separable-tensor theorem applies because $L/K$ is finite separable and $\widetilde\Omega$ is algebraically closed; it makes this algebra a finite product of copies of $\widetilde\Omega$. The finite-product spectrum theorem therefore identifies each point of $Z$ with a one-point open subscheme isomorphic over $\widetilde\Omega$ to $\operatorname{Spec}\widetilde\Omega$. Each point consequently has exactly one $\widetilde\Omega$-valued lift: the corresponding residue-field map is a $\widetilde\Omega$-algebra map $\widetilde\Omega\to\widetilde\Omega$ and must be the identity. By the fibre-product universal property and the spectrum anti-equivalence, these lifts are exactly the $K$-algebra embeddings $\phi:L\to\widetilde\Omega$. Concretely the associated point is the kernel of the evaluation map $L\otimes_K\widetilde\Omega\to\widetilde\Omega$, $a\otimes c\mapsto\phi(a)c$.

source.place: Tag 0FD1, lemma-baby-stein, finite separable tensor factors; algebra.tex Tag 00ED, lemma-spec-product; schemes.tex Tag 01I4, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes.

proof.text: Every embedding $\phi:L\to\widetilde\Omega$ of step 7 lands in $L\subset\Omega$. For $a\in L$, its minimal polynomial over $K$ splits into linear factors in $L[T]$ by normality. Applying $\phi$ to its equation shows that $\phi(a)$ is a root of this polynomial in $\widetilde\Omega$; the split factorization and absence of zero divisors imply that it equals one of the roots already in $L$. Conversely any $K$-embedding $L\to\Omega$ composes with $\Omega\subset\widetilde\Omega$. The two constructions are inverse. Thus the evaluation identification of step 7 is exactly with $\operatorname{Hom}_K(L,\Omega)$.

source.place: Tag 0BTD, finite Galois extension L/K; elementary use of its normality and the evaluation description of the geometric generic fibre.

proof.text: Write $t_\phi:\operatorname{Spec}\widetilde\Omega\to Y$ for the lift associated to $\phi:L\to\Omega$. On coordinate rings, $t_\phi\circ\operatorname{Spec}(\widetilde\sigma)$ corresponds to $a\mapsto\widetilde\sigma(\phi(a))=\sigma(\phi(a))$. It is therefore $t_{\sigma\circ\phi}$, proving the required equivariance, with precisely the action convention in the statement. Contravariance of $\operatorname{Spec}$ and the composition identity in step 6 verify the left action law. At the inclusion $\phi:L\subset\Omega$, the equality $\sigma\circ\phi=\phi$ is equivalent to $\sigma(a)=a$ for all $a\in L$, which defines $\operatorname{Aut}_L(\Omega)$. This is the asserted stabilizer.
